fatal_errors: The proposed intervention omits the target compositional adjustment—changing Fe/Co/Mn ratios and reducing phosphorus from 20 to 15 at.%—that produced eutectic-dominated solidification.
Neither cited source supports the central claim that a moderated cooling tail reduces free volume while avoiding crystallization, raises crystallization onset, or improves critical casting diameter.

A slower cooling tail can increase structural relaxation but also gives phosphides and other crystalline phases more time to nucleate, so improved glass-forming ability does not follow without evidence for a specific safe time-temperature window.
Critical casting diameter cannot be established by comparing fixed-geometry melt-spun specimens; samples spanning thickness or diameter and calibrated cooling rates are required.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the general problem and proposes a testable processing concept, but it is not a reconstruction of the reported result. The target combined a specific composition change with melt spinning at 40 m/s, yielding a fully amorphous approximately 20 μm ribbon while slower cooling produced partitioned phosphides and a solid solution. Its mechanism centered on suppressing primary crystallization, segregation, and phosphide nucleation and shifting solidification toward cooperative eutectic growth. The generated hypothesis instead invokes an unreported controlled cooling tail, free-volume reduction, and higher critical casting diameter. E1 supports rapid-quench amorphization and short-range order only; E2 supports the generic metastability and thermally activated crystallization of amorphous material. Neither validates gradient quenching or its claimed benefits. The proposed paired experiment could test crystallization onset, but direct free-volume measurements and a geometry series would be needed to distinguish relaxation from partial crystallization and to assess glass-forming ability.
